3.2.5.1-f62.text: Huc faciunt medicamenta Venerem sopientia, ut Camphora pudendis alligata, & in bracha gestata (quidam ait) membrum flaccidum reddit. Laboravit hoc morbo virgo nobilis, cui inter caetera praescripsit Medicus, ut laminam plumbeam multis foraminibus pertusam ad dies viginti portaret in dorso; ad exiccandum vero sperma jussit eam quam parcissime cibari, & manducare frequenter coriandrum praeparatum, et semen lactucae et acetosae, et sic eam a morbo liberavit. Porro impediunt & remittunt coitum folia salicis trita & epota, & si frequentius usurpentur ipsa in totum auferunt. Idem praestat Topatius annulo gestatus, dexterum lupi testiculum attritum, & oleo vel aqua rosata exhibitum Veneris taedium inducere scribit Alexander Benedictus: lac butyri commestum & semen Cannabis, & Camphora exhibita idem praestant. Verbena herba gestata libidinem extinguit, pulvisque ranae decollatae & exiccatae. Ad extinguendum coitum, ungantur membra genitalia, & renes & pecten aqua in qua opium Thebaicum sit dissolutum; libidini maxime contraria Camphora est, & coriandrum siccum frangit coitum, & erectionem virgae impedit; idem efficit synapium ebibitum. Da verbenam in potu et non erigetur virga sex diebus; utere mentha sicca cum aceto, genitalia illinita succo Hyoscyami aut cicutae, coitus appetitum sedant, &c. ℞ seminis lactuc. portulac. coriandri an. ʒ i, menthae siccae ʒ ß, sacchari albiss. ℥ iiii, pulveriscentur omnia subtiliter, & post ea simul misce aqua Nenupharis, f. confec. solida in morsulis. Ex his sumat mane unum quum surgat. Innumera fere his similia petas ab Hildesheimo loco praedicto, Mizaldo, Porta, caeterisque.

translations.note: 'Bracha' is taken as 'braca', breeches. 'Lac butyri' means buttermilk. 'Synapium' is 'sinapi', mustard. 'Pecten' means the pubic region. 'Nenuphar' is the water-lily. 'f. confec.' is read as 'fiat confectio' ('make a confection'). The passage is a compilation; Burton names Alexander Benedictus only for the remedy of the wolf's testicle, and he refers to Hildesheim, Mizaldus and Porta for more.
translations.text: To this purpose serve medicines that lull desire to sleep: camphor, for instance, bound to the privy parts and carried in the breeches (says one), makes the member flaccid. A noble maiden laboured under this disease, for whom the physician prescribed, among other things, that she should wear on her back for twenty days a plate of lead pierced with many holes; and to dry up the seed he ordered that she be fed as sparingly as possible and eat often of prepared coriander, and lettuce and sorrel seed; and so he freed her from the disease. Moreover, willow leaves bruised and drunk hinder and abate coition, and if used more often they take it away altogether. A topaz worn in a ring does the same; Alexander Benedictus writes that the right testicle of a wolf, ground and given in oil or rose-water, brings on a loathing of venery; buttermilk eaten, hemp seed, and camphor given do the same. The herb vervain carried about extinguishes lust, and so does the powder of a frog beheaded and dried. To extinguish coition, let the genitals, the kidneys and the pubic region be anointed with water in which Theban opium has been dissolved; camphor is the thing most contrary to lust, and dried coriander breaks coition and hinders the erection of the yard; mustard drunk does the same. Give vervain in drink and the yard will not rise for six days; use dried mint with vinegar; the genitals smeared with the juice of henbane or hemlock allay the appetite for coition, etc. Take of the seeds of lettuce, purslane and coriander, of each 1 drachm; of dried mint half a drachm; of the whitest sugar 4 ounces; let them all be finely powdered, and afterwards mix them together with water-lily water; make a solid confection in small morsels. Let him take one of these in the morning when he rises. You may find almost countless remedies like these in Hildesheim in the place aforesaid, in Mizaldus, Porta, and the rest.
